{{DISPLAYTITLE:The conserved thing is the thing that does the moving}}
{{Noether's theorems map}}

''Mathematical counterpart: [[Noether's theorems/Mathematics/Poisson brackets and the generator identity|Poisson brackets and the generator identity]].''

There is a way of setting up mechanics in which the connection between symmetry
and conservation stops being a theorem and becomes a piece of grammar. This page
explains that, and it is the shortest real explanation in the volume.

== Every quantity is also an instruction ==

In this setup, each measurable quantity does double duty.

It is a '''number''' you can measure — the energy, the momentum, the angular
momentum.

It is also an '''instruction''' for moving the system: a rule saying how
everything shifts if you nudge along that quantity.

The two roles are not related by analogy. They are the same object used two ways,
and the machinery is built so that specifying one specifies the other.

Momentum, as an instruction, says: slide everything sideways. Angular momentum
says: turn everything. Energy says: let time pass.

That last one deserves a moment. Energy is not just the quantity that time
symmetry conserves. Energy '''is''' the instruction "let time pass". Running the
system forward and asking about its energy are the same operation.

== The two-way street ==

Now there is one construction that takes two quantities and returns a number
measuring how much each one changes under the other's instruction.

And that construction has a property you can read straight off how it is built:
'''swap the two inputs and the answer flips sign.'''

Which means: how much A changes under B's instruction, and how much B changes
under A's instruction, are the same number with opposite signs. If one is zero,
the other is zero.

Put "the energy" in for B. Then:

'''"The quantity A does not change as time passes"''' and '''"the energy does not
change under A's instruction"''' are the same statement.

The first sentence says A is conserved. The second says the system is symmetric
under the transformation A generates.

They are not two facts joined by a theorem. They are one fact, written from either
end, and what joins them is that swapping the inputs flips the sign.

== Energy for free ==

Feed the energy in as both inputs.

Swapping two identical things must leave the answer alone. But swapping flips the
sign. A number that equals its own negative is zero.

So the energy does not change as time passes, and it took one sentence with no
physics in it.

'''Energy conservation is the sign-flip, applied to energy twice.'''

== What this does not replace ==

Two honest limits, because this page makes the connection look easier than it is.

'''It needs a setting that not every theory has.''' Getting into this framework
requires being able to solve for speeds in terms of momenta, and precisely the
theories the second theorem is about cannot. For those, this is the hard road.

'''It only ever gives you the on-shell statement.''' Everything above assumes the
system is doing what physics says. The identity that holds regardless — the whole
substance of
[[Noether's theorems/Explainers/True everywhere against true for real motions|the
identity page]] — never appears, because there is nowhere for it to live.

So this is a shorter route to less. It belongs beside Noether's argument, not
instead of it. But if you want one sentence for why symmetry and conservation
travel together, this page has it.

== The same grammar in quantum mechanics ==

The double life survives the move to quantum mechanics, and in a recognisable
form.

There, too, each measurable quantity is also an instruction for changing the
system. Momentum still says "slide everything". Energy still says "let time pass".
And there is still a construction taking two quantities and returning a measure of
how much each responds to the other's instruction.

It still flips sign when you swap the inputs. So the argument on this page runs
again, word for word, and the conclusion is the same: a quantity is conserved
exactly when the energy is unchanged by the motion that quantity generates.

This is worth knowing for two reasons.

It explains why the vocabulary carried over. Physicists say a symmetry is
"generated by" a conserved quantity in both classical and quantum contexts, and
they mean the same structural thing in each.

And it marks where the parallel stops. What quantum mechanics does not inherit is
the guarantee that a classical symmetry is still a symmetry after the move. That
question has its own answer, and sometimes the answer is no. See
[[Noether's theorems/Explainers/When a symmetry does not survive|When a symmetry
does not survive]].

counterpart page named above.''
